orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the December 13, 2017 order granting the dismissal branches of defendants' separate motions.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted summary judgment dismissing the complaint against each defendant.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped in a pothole in a parking lot on August 10, 2013. The lot abutted premises owned by McGuire and leased to Starbucks; those neighboring ownership and tenancy relationships do not identify the lot's owner.

legal_issues.finding: McGuire established nonownership of the accident lot and noncreation of its defect; Starbucks established no ownership, occupancy, control or special use. Plaintiff raised no triable issue against either defendant.
McGuire established that she did not create the alleged pothole defect; plaintiff raised no triable issue. The opinion does not separately make a creation finding about Starbucks.

evidence_discussed.description: Each defendant submitted evidence about its relationship to the accident lot, and McGuire about noncreation; the specific form of that evidence is not identified.

quality.notes: Private status of the actual parking lot is not established. Ownership/tenancy of the neighboring premises must not be transferred to the accident site; the court affirmatively found lack of relevant lot relationships. No public ownership is inferred. Defendant_roles describes expressly stated neighboring owner/tenant roles only. One appealed order resolves separate motions; affirmance insofar as appealed is not mixed. Plaintiff's customer/visitor role is unstated.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with one bill of costs.

On the morning of August 10, 2013, the plaintiff allegedly tripped and fell in a pothole located in a parking lot abutting premises in Suffolk County owned by the defendant Karen D. McGuire and leased to the defendant Starbucks Corporation.

The order, insofar as appealed from, granted those branches of the separate motions of the defendants which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.

Here, McGuire submitted evidence sufficient to establish, prima facie, that she did not own the parking lot where the accident occurred and that she did not create the alleged defect that caused the plaintiff to fall

With respect to Starbucks Corporation, it submitted evidence sufficient to establish, prima facie, that it did not own, occupy, control, or make special use of the parking lot where the accident occurred, and that it cannot be held liable for the plaintiff's alleged injuries
"However, as a general matter, an owner owes no duty to warn or to protect others from a defective or dangerous condition on neighboring premises, unless the owner had created or contributed to it"
Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to award the defendants summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.

orders.description: Miller's Ale House's appeal from the February 8, 2019 order limited to denial of dismissal of the complaint against it.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against Miller's Ale House.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell inside Miller's Ale House's restaurant. A warning sign was present near the accident scene, but the opinion does not identify the hazardous substance or condition.

legal_issues.finding: A warning sign satisfied the warning duty but did not establish that appropriate remedial measures were taken within a reasonable time after actual notice.
The court stated noncreation as part of the initial summary-judgment burden; it did not separately determine who created the hazard, instead resolving the motion on remedial action after notice.

The court addressed remedial action after actual notice and held defendants failed to negate an accident caused by a failure to act appropriately within a reasonable time. It did not make a final liability finding.
Constructive notice appears in the governing initial-burden rule; no separate constructive-notice determination is made because the application concerns actual notice and remedial action.

evidence_discussed.description: The court discusses a warning sign near the scene. It does not identify the form of the evidence establishing the sign's presence.

quality.notes: Private restaurant control is supported by the named defendant's restaurant and the court's discussion of its warning/remediation duties; title ownership is not inferred. A warning sign does not establish water, a spill or any particular hazard, so hazards remains unclear. Indoor_floor maps the stated interior slip without inventing a specific room. Only Miller's appealed branch is evaluated. Plaintiff's role and accident date are unstated.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.
to recover damages for personal injuries that he allegedly sustained when he slipped and fell inside Miller's Ale House's restaurant.
The order, insofar as appealed from, denied that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Miller's Ale House.

Here, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the plaintiff, the defendants failed to establish, prima facie, that the accident was not the result of Miller's Ale House's failure to take appropriate remedial measures within a reasonable period of time after acquiring actual notice of a hazardous condition
The presence of a warning sign in the vicinity of the accident scene merely satisfied Miller's Ale House's duty to warn of a dangerous condition

"A defendant who moves for summary judgment in a slip-and-fall case has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that it neither created the hazardous condition nor had actual or constructive notice of its existence for a sufficient length of time to discover and remedy it"

Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination denying that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against Miller's Ale House.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the February 16, 2017 order granting defendants summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff testified that she tripped over a raised rubber mat near the entrance inside defendants' supermarket. Her husband described the raised portion as two fat fingers high; the store manager estimated approximately half an inch.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants' evidence, including surveillance footage, failed to establish the mat condition was physically insignificant and nonactionable under all the circumstances; dangerousness was not conclusively found.
Defendants failed to establish that plaintiff did not know what caused her fall; her deposition identified a raised mat.

The trial court improperly granted summary judgment on a causation-identification ground defendants had not raised. The appellate court also addressed substantive causation and trivial-defect sufficiency.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff's deposition identified the raised mat as the cause of her trip.
Husband and store-manager depositions gave differing height descriptions; neither measurement is treated as conclusively established.
Defendants submitted surveillance footage of the incident; the court found their evidence insufficient to establish a trivial defect. The footage itself was not independently viewed.

quality.notes: The procedural error is ancillary to substantive review of causation and triviality, so this is not a procedural-only exclusion. Full reversal denying the dismissal motion favors plaintiff at this stage, not a final finding of negligence. Supermarket attribution and defendants' store manager support private retail control without title ownership. Plaintiff's customer/visitor status and accident date are unstated.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint is denied.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she fell inside the defendants' supermarket in Poughkeepsie.
The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint.
The plaintiff gave deposition testimony to the effect that she tripped and fell over a raised portion of a rubber mat near the entrance of the supermarket.

The plaintiff's husband testified at his deposition that the raised portion of the mat was "two fat fingers high." The defendants' store manager testified at his deposition that the bump in the mat was about half an inch high.

Here, the Supreme Court should not have granted the motion on the ground that the plaintiff did not know what caused her to fall, since the issue was not raised by the defendants in their motion papers.
In any event, the defendants failed to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff did not know what caused her to fall

Here, the evidence submitted by the defendants, including a surveillance footage of the incident, was insufficient to demonstrate, prima facie, that the condition of the mat was trivial as a matter of law and therefore not actionable

Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint, without considering the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers

"A defendant seeking dismissal of a complaint on the basis that the alleged defect is trivial must make a prima facie showing that the defect is, under the circumstances, physically insignificant and that the characteristics of the defect or the surrounding circumstances do not increase the risks it poses. Only then does the burden shift to the plaintiff to establish an issue of fact"

orders.description: Estate representative's appeal from the July 18, 2017 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the substituted defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff, a long-term upstairs tenant, fell down an interior stairway in Robinson's two-family house on March 7, 2010. Alleged conditions included a loose top step, a loose screw on the landing and inadequate lighting.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the obligation of an owner or possessor/controller to maintain reasonably safe property.
Noncreation was stated as part of the initial burden; the application does not separately resolve whether the owner created the alleged conditions.
The court included actual notice in the initial-burden standard but did not separately determine actual notice in its application.
Defendant failed to establish that Robinson lacked constructive notice of the alleged step, screw and lighting conditions; notice was not conclusively established.
Defendant failed to establish that the alleged conditions were not a proximate cause; the court did not conclusively identify which condition caused the fall.

quality.notes: Private ownership and tenancy are explicit, but the actual-case text describes only falling down stairs; it does not specify a slip or trip. Loose-step/screw/lighting allegations do not establish that mechanism. Reason other denotes unresolved mechanism, not definite out-of-scope status or lack of a negligence finding. Defendant_roles preserves original owner Robinson and substituted executor as other; it does not assert the executor personally owned the house. Specific evidence types are not identified. Ordinary substitution history is not treated as an adjudicated procedural dispute.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

On March 7, 2010, at approximately 8:00 p.m., the plaintiff allegedly sustained personal injuries when she fell down an interior stairway in a two-family house that was owned by Sheila Robinson and in which the plaintiff had rented the upstairs apartment for more than 20 years.
The order denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The plaintiff commenced this action against Robinson to recover damages for personal injuries, alleging that Robinson was negligent in, among other things, failing to provide adequate lighting in the subject stairway. During the pendency of the action, Robinson died, and Eric Alleyne, as executor of her estate, was substituted as the defendant.
A property owner, or a party in possession or control of real property, has a duty to maintain the property in a reasonably safe condition

"In a premises liability case, a defendant [real] property owner, or a party in possession or control of real property, who moves for summary judgment has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that it neither created the alleged defective condition nor had actual or constructive notice [*2] of its existence"

Here, contrary to the defendant's contention, he failed to demonstrate, prima facie, inter alia, that Robinson lacked constructive notice of the alleged defective conditions, including a loose top step, a loose screw on the landing of the subject staircase, and inadequate lighting in the staircase, or that these conditions were not a proximate cause of the plaintiff's fall
Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to deny the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Best Buy's limited appeal from the June 7, 2010 order denying dismissal of the claim against it.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied Best Buy's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped over protruding concrete on the ground in an area adjacent to Best Buy's store. The opinion identifies store ownership but does not specify the type or ownership of the adjacent accident area.

legal_issues.finding: The court distinguished the reasonably-safe-premises duty from conditions both open/obvious and not inherently dangerous; Best Buy did not establish that exception.
Best Buy failed to establish as a matter of law that the concrete condition was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous.
Best Buy failed to show the concrete was a natural topographic condition or otherwise beyond what a landowner could reasonably remedy; the court did not finally find liability.

evidence_discussed.description: Best Buy submitted evidence on obviousness and inherent danger, but the opinion does not identify its specific form.

quality.notes: Store ownership does not establish private ownership/control of the adjacent ground where plaintiff fell. Retain review without assuming sidewalk, parking lot or public property; location other reflects unspecified adjacent ground. Retail describes the associated store setting, and defendant_roles owner refers only to the store. The source's L.E typography is preserved in evidence rather than silently repaired. The affirmed limited appeal is not mixed. Plaintiff's role and accident date are unknown.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell over a cluster of concrete protruding from the ground in an area adjacent to a store owned by the defendant Best Buy Stores, L.E (hereinafter Best Buy).

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant Best Buy Stores, L.E, appeals, as limited by its brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Iannacci, J.), entered June 7, 2010, as denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

While a landowner has a duty to maintain its premises in a reasonably safe manner (see Basso v Miller, 40 NY2d 233 [1976]), it does not have a duty to protect against an open and obvious condition which, as a matter of law, is not inherently dangerous

The evidence submitted by Best Buy in support of its motion was insufficient to establish, as a matter of law, that the condition that caused the plaintiff to fall was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous

Best Buy failed to demonstrate that the cluster of concrete on which the plaintiff tripped was a naturally occurring topographic condition or some other condition that a landowner could not reasonably be expected to remedy, and thus failed to show that it was not inherently dangerous
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied Best Buy’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.
